books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Thomas Nast, “The Union as It Was — The Lost Cause, Worse than Slavery,” Harper’s Weekly, October 24, 1874

stimulus.text: Thomas Nast’s cartoon “The Union as It Was — The Lost Cause, Worse than Slavery,” Harper’s Weekly, October 24, 1874. A man marked “White League,” a rifle on his back, shakes hands with a hooded Klansman marked “K.K.” over a shield. Above them an eagle carries the words “The Union as It Was” and “This Is a White Man’s Government.” Inside the shield, a Black mother and father crouch over their baby in grief, while behind them a freedman hangs from a tree and a schoolhouse burns. A child’s primer lies dropped on the ground.
stimulus.source_note: Thomas Nast, “The Union as It Was — The Lost Cause, Worse than Slavery,” Harper’s Weekly, October 24, 1874, p. 878 (Library of Congress, LCCN2001696840). Public domain. Image viewed before writing; details described from the image itself.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Nast’s cartoon most directly argues that

options.text: white terrorist groups were undoing Reconstruction by violence.
the federal government had already withdrawn its troops from the South.
options.misconception: Background: federal troops stayed in the South until 1877, three years after the cartoon.

options.text: Black Southerners welcomed the return of Democratic rule.
options.misconception: The grieving family at the center shows fear, not welcome.

options.text: the White League and the Ku Klux Klan were enemies of each other.
options.misconception: The two men shake hands, so the cartoon shows them as partners, not enemies.

rationales.A: The White League man and the Klansman clasp hands over a grieving Black family, with a lynching and a burning schoolhouse behind them. Nast shows two violent groups working together to crush the freedom Reconstruction promised.
rationales.B: Background: federal troops stayed in the South until 1877, three years after the cartoon.
rationales.C: The grieving family at the center shows fear, not welcome.
rationales.D: The two men shake hands, so the cartoon shows them as partners, not enemies.
rationales.general:
1. The handshake is the cartoon’s center: the White League and the Klan join hands.
2. Above them the eagle proclaims a white man’s government, and below them a Black family grieves.
3. Behind the family, a man hangs from a tree and a schoolhouse burns.
4. Nast is not reporting a single crime; he is showing a system of terror at work.
Remember: a cartoon’s handshake can name an alliance that words alone would take a paragraph to prove.
